clinician.trajectory_summary: A 13-year-old boy presented with a 5mm entry wound on the lower sternum after an accidental air rifle chest injury, experiencing chest pain. Initial plain chest X-ray and extended FAST scan did not reveal a lodged pellet in the chest but showed minimal pericardial effusion. Four hours post-admission, the patient developed neurological symptoms including generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, reduced consciousness, and left-sided weakness. A CECT of the head, neck, and thorax confirmed a pellet embolism in the right internal carotid artery, located within the carotid foramen, with non-opacification of the right internal carotid artery and proximal carotid artery suggesting a thrombus causing an acute cerebral infarction in the right cerebral territory. The CECT also showed minimal pericardial and pleural effusion, which was consistent with a 2D echocardiogram finding of thin pericardial effusion. Due to acute cerebral edema resulting from the cerebral infarction, a decompressive craniotomy was performed. A four-vessel cerebral Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) was conducted, but attempts to retrieve the tightly wedged pellet and aspirate the thrombus in the proximal ICA were unsuccessful. The DSA also revealed no cross-circulation from the left ICA. After two weeks of inpatient care, the patient sustained permanent hemiplegia and was transferred to a rehabilitation center.
